reels.title: Function, dict or class: the kitchen view

beats.say: Why would you build a whole restaurant just to make toast?

show.kicker: Pick the simplest tool that works

beats.say: Think of a kitchen. A recipe card is a function. Ingredients go in, a dish comes out, and nothing is remembered afterward.

A shopping list is like a dict, short for dictionary. It is just labelled facts you read: milk, two. Eggs, twelve. A dataclass is the same list on a printed form, so every field has a name and a place.

show.title: A list is a *dict*, a form is a dataclass

beats.say: A class is a cashier with a till. It remembers how much money is inside, and it refuses to give change it does not have. That memory plus the rules is what makes a class worth it.

check.q: In the kitchen picture, which thing most needs to be a class?
opts: A recipe card that turns eggs into an omelette
A cashier whose till total changes and who must refuse bad requests
A shopping list read once at the shop
check.why: A class earns its place when it holds changing state and guards rules. The recipe is a function and the list is a dict or dataclass.

work: Look at one class in your code and ask whether it holds any changing state.
Name one function that could stay a plain function.

reels.title: The five-row decision table

beats.say: You are passing the same five values to six functions. Is that a problem?
Start simple. A transformation with no state, like converting cents to dollars, is a function. Same input, same output, nothing to remember.
A record that is only read, say a trip with an id, a fare and a pickup time, is a dict. Better, a dataclass, because a typo in a field name then fails loudly instead of silently returning nothing.
Once data has rules, like fare is never negative, or state changes over time, like a rate limiter counting requests per minute, use a class. It holds the state and guards the rules in one place.
Five values times six functions is thirty places to get it wrong. Bundle them into one object and there is one place.

show.title: Bundle repeated values
items: Same five values everywhere means an object is hiding
One object means one place for rules
Thirty chances to err become one

check.q: You pass user_id, rate, window and count to six functions that update a counter. What is the best move?
opts: Convert them all to global variables
Bundle them into a class with methods
Store them in a dict and keep the six functions
check.why: Repeated values with changing state and rules want to be an object, so the rules live in one place.

work: Search your code for parameter groups repeated across several functions.
Replace one hand-passed dict of records with a dataclass.

reels.title: Where dicts and classes bite back

beats.say: Why does a dict let a fare of minus fifty slip through, while a class does not?
A dict accepts anything. A typo like fare underscore amt quietly creates a new key, and the real one stays empty. A dataclass catches the wrong name, but by default it still does not check values.
To enforce rules, validate in the constructor. For dataclasses that is a method called post init. Reject bad data at the door, so every object that exists is valid.

Two traps. Mutable state shared between instances, like one list reused as a default by every object, leaks data across them. And records that anyone can change later break your rules, so freeze them with a frozen dataclass.

show.title: Gotchas interviewers probe
items: Shared mutable default leaks data between objects
Rules checked only at creation break if fields change later
A class with no state is a function in disguise

check.q: Why can a validated dataclass still end up holding a negative fare?
opts: Dataclasses cannot hold numbers
Validation ran only at creation and the field was changed afterward
Dicts are always safer
check.why: Checking in post init protects only construction. If the field is mutable, later assignment bypasses it, so freeze it or validate in setters.

work: Add a post init check for one invariant, such as fare at least zero.
Mark read-only records as frozen dataclasses.
Grep for list or dict default arguments.

reels.title: Choosing by what changes

beats.say: When is a class the wrong answer, and when is it the only answer?

Wrong: wrapping a stateless transform in a class. It adds ceremony and hides that the logic is pure and easy to test. Also wrong at scale. A million small Python objects can eat hundreds of megabytes, where columnar data needs a fraction.
Right: several interchangeable behaviours, like sinks or LLM providers. Give each small class the same method name, such as write, and callers never change when you add a new one.

chip.text: Add a sink, change nothing else

beats.say: So choose by what changes. Pure logic, a function. Bulk records, dataframes or typed schemas. Rules with evolving state, or swappable behaviours, a class.

show.title: Choose by what changes
items: Bulk records: dataframe or typed schema
Swappable behaviours: small classes, one method name

check.q: You must support three output destinations and add more later. What fits best?
opts: One big function with an if branch per destination
A dict of settings only
Small classes sharing one method name, one per destination
check.why: Interchangeable behaviours behind a shared method let callers stay unchanged when a new destination is added.

work: Find one if-chain that picks behaviour by type and consider replacing it with classes sharing a method.
Check whether any pipeline holds millions of rows as Python objects instead of columnar data.

reels.title: A class is a blank form

beats.say: Why do programmers write a class, when a plain list of values would do?

show.sub: instead of a loose list of values

beats.say: Think of a class as a blank trip form. It says every trip needs an id, a fare, and a distance. Each time you fill one in, you get one real trip. The blank form is the class. Each filled copy is called an instance.

The form can also have rules. If someone writes a negative fare, the form refuses it straight away. It can also do small jobs for you, like working out fare per kilometre. A job that belongs to the form is called a method.
So a class keeps the data and its rules together, in one place, and every copy follows them.

check.q: In the form analogy, what is an instance?
opts: The blank form itself
One filled-in copy of the form
The rule that refuses bad values
The printed description of a trip
check.why: The class is the blank form. Each filled-in copy, such as one particular trip, is an instance.

work: Find a place in your code where a dictionary is passed around and ask which keys it must always have.
List the rules one record must obey, such as no negative fare, and see where they are checked today.

reels.title: What happens when you call Trip

beats.say: What really happens when you call Trip with seven, one hundred twenty, and eight?

Python makes an empty object, then runs the special method named init on it. Init receives the object as its first argument, called self, plus your three values. It checks the fare is not negative, then stores trip id, fare, and km on self.

Now call fare per km on that trip. Python quietly rewrites it as Trip dot fare per km, passing the trip as self. So self is not magic. It is just the trip you called the method on. With fare one twenty and eight kilometres, the answer is fifteen.
Last, repr controls how the trip prints, so a failing test shows Trip seven, fare one twenty, instead of a useless memory address.

check.q: When you write t.fare_per_km(), what is self inside the method?
opts: The class Trip
A copy of the fare
The object t
A new empty trip
check.why: Python passes the instance the method was called on as the first argument, so self is t.

work: Add a repr to any class you own, then print a list of its objects in a test.
Write a tiny class with a check in init and test that bad values raise an error.

reels.title: Where a class still leaks

beats.say: Your class rejects a negative fare, so why can a bad trip still sneak in later?

Because init only checks at birth. Anyone can write t dot fare equals minus five afterwards, and Python allows it. The rule is guarded once, not forever. To guard it always, use a property with a setter that repeats the check.

chip.text: Use a property setter to re-check

beats.say: Another gotcha: fare per km divides by km. The code returns zero when km is zero, which avoids a crash but hides bad data. A trip of zero kilometres might deserve an error instead. Choose on purpose.

show.title: Silent zero vs loud error
items: Zero km avoids a divide-by-zero crash
But a fake 0.0 flows downstream unnoticed
Decide: default value or raise an error

beats.say: Also, if init raises, no object is returned, so you never hold a half-built trip. And two trips with identical values are still not equal, unless you define equality, because the default compares identity.

show.title: Two more gotchas
items: Init raises: no object, no half-built trip

check.q: A Trip checks fare is not negative in init. What can still happen?
opts: Nothing, the check runs on every change
Someone sets t.fare to a negative number later and Python allows it
The Trip object is created half built
Python refuses to create any second trip
check.why: Init validates only at creation. Plain attributes can be reassigned freely, so use a property setter or a frozen design to keep the rule.

work: Review classes that validate in init and ask whether attributes can be changed afterwards.
Decide for each divide-by-zero guard whether a default or an error is the honest answer.
Add a test that two trips with the same values compare as you expect.

reels.title: When not to hand-write the class

beats.say: Should every record in your pipeline be a hand-written class?

Not always. A plain class like Trip needs init, repr, and ideally equality, all boilerplate. A dataclass generates them from three lines, and a frozen one blocks later changes. Use that by default for simple records.

Scale matters too. Millions of Python objects each carry a dictionary of attributes, costing roughly a hundred bytes or more apiece. For bulk data, keep columns in Arrow, pandas, or Spark, and validate with a schema at the boundary.
Reserve hand-written classes for things with behaviour and rules, like a fare calculator, where the logic deserves a home and tests.

show.title: Choose by job
items: Behaviour and rules: a real class

check.q: You must process 50 million trip rows. What is the best default?
opts: One hand-written Trip object per row
Columnar data such as Arrow or Spark, validated by a schema
A list of dictionaries
One giant class with every method
check.why: Per-object memory and loop overhead in Python grow painfully at tens of millions of rows. Columnar structures are compact and fast, and a schema validates at the boundary.

work: Replace simple hand-written record classes with frozen dataclasses where it fits.
Check whether any job builds millions of Python objects and measure its memory.
Keep real classes for logic that needs rules, tests, and a clear home.

reels.title: The blank card Python prints for you

beats.say: How much boring writing would you do to make a simple form? Python can print the form for you.

show.sub: so you don't write it by hand

beats.say: Think of a library card. Every card has the same boxes: name, member number, expiry date. A dataclass is that blank card. You list the boxes once, and Python builds the rest: how to fill one in, how to print it, and how to check if two cards match.
Now laminate the card. Nobody can scribble over it. That is a frozen dataclass. Because it can never change, you can safely hand the same card to many people, and use it as a key in a filing index.

chip.text: Can't change, so safe to share

check.q: In the library card analogy, what does laminating the card stand for?
opts: A frozen dataclass that cannot be changed
Printing the card faster
Checking two cards match
Adding more boxes
check.why: Lamination means nobody can edit the card, which matches frozen=True. That is why it is safe to share and to use as a key.

work: Find a class in your code that only holds fields and has hand-written init and repr. Note it as a dataclass candidate.
Pick one value that should never change after creation, such as a currency amount or a config, and mark it as frozen.

reels.title: What the decorator writes for you

beats.say: You write four lines of class. How does Python hand you a constructor, a printout and an equality check for free?

show.title: Four lines in

beats.say: The decorator reads your type annotated fields, in order. From them it generates init, repr and eq. So Batch of orders prints as Batch, table equals orders, and two batches with the same fields compare equal. Without it, equality would just compare memory addresses.

Money is the classic example. Store amount as an integer in paise, so five hundred rupees is fifty thousand, never a float. Set frozen true, and assigning to amount raises an error. Frozen also makes the object hashable, so it works in sets and as a dict key. Add order true and a list of Money sorts by its fields.

show.title: Money as a value object
items: amount is an int in paise: 500 rupees is 50000
Frozen means hashable: sets and dict keys work
order=True: instances sort by their fields

check.q: Why does frozen=True let a dataclass be used as a dict key?
opts: It makes the object hashable because it can't change
It converts the object to a string
It sorts the fields
It copies the object on each lookup
check.why: A dict key needs a stable hash. Frozen fields can't change, so the hash stays valid and Python generates one.

work: Replace float money fields with an integer in the smallest unit, wrapped in a frozen Money dataclass.
Use order=True on a small value type and sort a list of them instead of writing a key function.

reels.title: Gotchas that interviewers probe

beats.say: What happens if you write rows colon list equals empty brackets in a dataclass?

Python refuses, with a ValueError, because one shared list would be the default for every instance, so every batch would append into the same rows. Use field with default factory set to list. The factory runs once per instance, giving each batch its own list.

Next gotcha: validation. The generated init does no checking, so put checks in post init, which runs right after it. Raise ValueError if table is empty. Also, frozen is shallow. A frozen object holding a list can still have that list mutated, and hashing it will fail. Type hints are not enforced either: pass a string for amount and nothing complains.

show.title: Three more caveats
items: __post_init__ runs after init: put validation there
Frozen is shallow: a list inside can still change
A frozen object with a list field can't be hashed
Type hints are not enforced at runtime

check.q: You need each Batch to start with its own empty list of rows. What is correct?
opts: rows: list = []
rows: list = field(default_factory=list)
rows: list = None, then never set it
rows: list = list
check.why: default_factory runs for every new instance, so each gets a fresh list. A literal empty list would be one shared object.

work: Search your dataclasses for list, dict or set defaults and switch them to default_factory.
Move input checks, such as non-empty names and positive amounts, into __post_init__.
Before freezing a class, check it has no mutable fields that break the immutability promise.

reels.title: Dataclass, Pydantic or dict?

beats.say: Dataclass, Pydantic, or plain dict? Which one should model your data?

show.sub: pick by where the data comes from

beats.say: Use a dataclass inside your own code, where types are already trusted. It is light, standard library, and fast. Use Pydantic at the boundary, where untrusted data enters: API payloads, tool inputs, structured model output. There it coerces types and rejects bad values, at the price of a dependency and slower construction.

Prefer frozen value objects for money, keys and config. They are safe to share across threads and cache. Skip dataclasses when an object has rich behaviour and hidden state, or when millions of rows per second matter: then use tuples, slots, or columnar tools like Arrow instead of one Python object per row.

show.title: When to choose what
items: Frozen value objects: money, keys, config
Rich behaviour or hidden state: a normal class
Millions of rows a second: tuples, slots or Arrow
Untrusted input: Pydantic at the boundary

check.q: You process 50 million rows a second in a hot loop. What is the best fit?
opts: One Pydantic model per row
One frozen dataclass per row
A columnar format such as Arrow, not one object per row
A dict per row with validation on every access
check.why: At that scale, per-row Python objects cost too much memory and time. Columnar data processes whole batches with far less overhead.

work: Draw the boundary in one service: validate with Pydantic where data enters, then pass plain dataclasses inward.
Benchmark object-per-row against a columnar approach before choosing a model for any high-volume path.

reels.title: One socket, many plugs

beats.say: Why does len work on a list, a word, and a dictionary, when they are totally different things?
Think of a power socket. Any appliance with the right plug just works, and the wall never needs to know if it is a kettle or a lamp.
Python is the wall. Special methods are the plug shapes. A class that has a length method fits the len socket. One with an add method fits the plus socket.
So you write the plug once, and everyone else uses the familiar socket. Nobody has to learn your custom method names.

check.q: What is a special method, in the socket analogy?
opts: The plug shape that lets your object fit a built-in socket like len
A faster version of a normal method
A method that only Python itself can define
check.why: Special methods are the agreed shapes Python looks for, so your object works with built-in syntax.

work: Pick one class you use daily and list which built-ins callers wish it supported.
Notice in code review where callers use a custom method name when len or in would read better.

reels.title: What len of x really does

beats.say: What really happens when you write len of x?
Python does not look inside x. It asks the type of x for a method named double underscore len, and calls it. If you wrote it, you get a number back. If not, you get a TypeError.

Take a buffer holding three readings. Define len to return three, and len of buffer gives three. Define iter, and a for loop walks the readings. Define contains, and the in operator answers yes or no.
Same idea for money. Define add, and five dollars plus ten dollars calls add and returns fifteen dollars. Define getitem, and square brackets work too.

check.q: What does Python do for the expression a + b?
opts: Calls a.__add__(b) on a's type
Copies the fields of a and b together
Calls len on both objects
check.why: Operators are translated into calls to the matching special method.

work: Add __len__ and __iter__ to a small container class and delete its custom count and items helpers.
Write a Money class with __add__ and __eq__ and test it with simple examples.

reels.title: Dunder gotchas

beats.say: You defined equals on your class, and suddenly it cannot go in a set. Why?

Because Python sets hash to none when you define equals alone. Equal objects must share a hash, and Python cannot guess yours. Define hash from the same fields you compare, or keep the object unhashable on purpose.
Another trap: add with the wrong type. Do not raise an error. Return NotImplemented, so Python tries the other side's reflected add before giving up.

show.title: Be polite with other types

beats.say: Also, truth tests fall back to len, so an empty container is false. And with only getitem, a for loop still works, counting zero, one, two, until an index error.

check.q: Your __add__ receives an unsupported type. What is best?
opts: Raise ValueError
Return NotImplemented
Return None
check.why: NotImplemented lets Python try the other operand's reflected method and then raise a clean TypeError.

work: Check every class that defines __eq__ and decide whether it needs __hash__ or should stay unhashable.
Add a test that an empty instance of your container is falsy, and that bad operand types raise TypeError.

reels.title: When dunders are a trap

beats.say: Your teammate overloads plus to mean send this message. Good design or trap?

Trap. Special methods hide cost and meaning behind familiar syntax. A len that runs a database query, or an in check that scans a million rows, looks free at the call site and is not. Keep dunders cheap and unsurprising.
Use them for value types and containers, where the meaning is obvious: money, ranges, buffers. For actions with side effects, write a named method like send or flush. The name documents the cost.

Before hand-writing everything, reach for dataclasses, which generate equals, or the collections abc Sequence, which gives contains, iteration and reversed from just getitem and len. Less code, fewer bugs.

check.q: Which use of a special method is the riskiest design?
opts: __len__ on a fixed-size buffer
__add__ on a Money value type
__len__ that issues a database query each call
check.why: Callers assume len is cheap and safe; hiding I/O behind it surprises them and hurts performance.

work: In review, flag any dunder that does I/O or has side effects and give it a named method.
Prefer dataclass or collections.abc base classes before hand-writing equality, ordering or sequence methods.

reels.title: A property is a worked-out answer

beats.say: What if you could ask a question and get a calculated answer, without ever seeing the calculation?

show.text: Looks like a fact. Is really a sum.
show.sub: Ask, and the answer is worked out for you

beats.say: Picture a taxi meter. You never ask the driver to do the sum. You just glance at the cost per kilometre, and it is worked out from the fare and the distance.
In Python, a property is that glance. The caller reads it like a plain fact, but behind it a small method runs and does the sum.

show.title: Reads like a fact, runs a *method*

beats.say: It can also guard the door. A property with no setter is read only. You can look at the value, but you cannot overwrite it.

show.title: Look, but do not *touch*
items: Writing to it raises an error
A setter can refuse nonsense values

check.q: A property has no setter. What happens when someone assigns a value to it?
opts: The value is stored silently
Python raises an AttributeError
The method runs again and ignores the value
check.why: Without a setter the property is read only, so assignment fails loudly with an AttributeError instead of quietly corrupting the object.

work: Find one method in your code that is called only to compute a value from stored fields, and note if it could be a property.
Explain a property to a teammate using the taxi meter picture.

reels.title: How a property computes on read

beats.say: How can reading trip dot fare per kilometre give 12 point 5, with no brackets?
Mark a method with the property decorator. Python then runs it whenever the name is read. A trip with fare 100 and 8 kilometres computes 100 divided by 8, rounded to two places: 12 point 5.

show.title: The decorator
show.note: Read the name, the method runs

beats.say: Nothing is stored. Change the fare to 120 and the next read gives 15, so the value can never go stale.
Try to assign to it and Python raises an attribute error, because no setter exists. Add a setter and you can check a value on assignment, while callers keep writing the same plain line.

check.q: A trip has fare 100 and 8 km. The fare is then changed to 120. What does fare_per_km return on the next read?
opts: 12.5, the value cached at creation
15.0, recomputed from the current fare
An AttributeError
check.why: A plain property stores nothing. It runs the method on each read, so it uses the current fare: 120 divided by 8 is 15.

work: Replace a stored, hand-updated derived field with a property so it cannot drift out of sync.
Add a guard for zero or missing denominators in every ratio property.

reels.title: Property traps interviewers probe

beats.say: Why can a harmless looking property crash your program with a recursion error?

show.sub: From a setter that looks innocent

beats.say: Because a setter that assigns to its own public name calls itself forever. Store the real value under an underscore name, like underscore fare, and let the property guard it.

chip.text: set fare inside set fare loops forever

beats.say: That underscore is only a convention. Python does not stop anyone reading it. Also, if the constructor assigns through the public name, the setter validates there too, so bad data is rejected at birth.

show.title: Convention and construction
items: Underscore means please do not touch
It is not enforced by Python
Assign via the public name in init to validate early

beats.say: Last, a property runs on every read. Divide by a zero distance and it crashes, so guard it. And a database call here would run on every glance, silently.

chip.text: Looks cheap, costs a call each time

check.q: A setter for fare contains the line self.fare = value after a check. What happens?
opts: It infinitely recurses, because it calls the same setter
It stores the value normally
The property becomes read only
check.why: Assigning to self.fare inside the fare setter triggers the setter again, forever. Store to a separate name such as _fare.

work: Review every setter and confirm it writes to a separate underscore attribute.
Search for properties that touch files, networks or databases and turn them into explicit methods.

reels.title: When to use properties, and when not

beats.say: Should every attribute get a getter and setter, just in case?

show.text: Getters and setters, just in case?

beats.say: No. Start with plain attributes. If you later need logic, turn one into a property, and no caller changes. That is the real payoff: you can defer the decision without breaking anyone.
Know the limits. Anything slow, like a query or an API call, belongs in an explicit method, where the name warns of the cost. For a costly value read many times, cache it once with cached property.

chip.text: Readers assume attribute access is cheap

beats.say: For validating records at a pipeline boundary, a schema library or frozen data class is cleaner than hand written setters. Use properties for small derived values, not as your validation framework.

show.title: Choose the right tool
items: Schema library or frozen data class: validate records at the boundary

check.q: Which is the best fit for a plain property?
opts: Fetching a driver's rating from the database
Fare per km computed from two stored numbers
Calling a web API for today's exchange rate
check.why: A property should be cheap and side-effect free. Dividing two stored numbers fits. Queries and API calls should be explicit methods so the cost is visible.

work: Add a review rule: no I/O or side effects inside a property.
Use cached_property or an explicit method for expensive derived values, and note when the cache could go stale.
Validate incoming pipeline records with a schema tool instead of custom setters.

reels.title: Labels on the boxes

beats.say: Ever opened a moving box with no label, and found kitchen knives inside?
A type hint is a label on the box. It says what goes in, and what comes out. Python itself never reads the label. It just runs your code anyway.
But a checker tool, like mypy, or your editor, reads every label before the code runs. Promise a number, hand over a word, and it flags the mistake, like a mover stopping at the door.
So the label does two jobs. It tells the next person what you meant. And it catches mistakes early, while they are still cheap to fix.

show.title: Two jobs
items: Documents intent for the next reader

check.q: What does Python do with type hints when it runs your code?
opts: Rejects wrong types
Ignores them; tools like mypy use them
Converts values to the hinted type
check.why: Hints are notes for people and checkers. Python does not enforce them at runtime.

work: Add hints to the signature of one function you wrote this week.
Run mypy or turn on your editor's type checking and read what it flags.

reels.title: Reading a typed signature

beats.say: What does a function signature with hints actually promise?
Take top cities. It takes a list of dicts, and an int k, defaulting to three. It returns a list of pairs, each a city name and a count. Anyone reading it knows the shape without opening the body.

show.title: Shape without the body
show.text: def top_cities(trips: list[dict], k: int = 3) -> list[tuple[str, int]]: ...

beats.say: Now find. It returns a Trip or None. That pipe None means it may come back empty. The checker then forces you to handle the empty case before you touch the trip, which stops the classic none has no attribute crash.

Last, Iterable and Callable. Iterable says anything you can loop over. Callable says a function taking a dict and returning a dict. Accept general types like Iterable, so lists, sets and generators all work.

show.title: Accept general, return specific
items: Iterable: anything you can loop over
Callable: a function dict in, dict out
Lists, sets, generators all fit Iterable

check.q: A function returns Trip | None. What does the checker make you do?
opts: Handle None before using the trip
Convert None to zero
Nothing, it only warns at runtime
check.why: The checker flags any use of the result that assumes it is not None, preventing attribute errors on None.

work: Mark every function that can return nothing with | None.
Change list parameters to Iterable where you only loop over them.

reels.title: When hints lie

beats.say: If Python ignores type hints, what stops a wrong one from running?

Nothing. At runtime the hints are just notes. Pass a string where an int was promised, and Python happily runs it, and may fail ten lines later with a confusing error. Only the checker, run in your editor or in the build, catches it.

Two gotchas. First, a bare list of dict says nothing about the keys inside, so a typo in a key still slips through. A typed dictionary or a class fixes that. Second, hints can lie. If the function can return None and you wrote Trip, the checker trusts you.

show.title: Two gotchas
items: list of dict hides the keys: use a typed dict or class
A hint can lie, and the checker trusts it

beats.say: So run the checker in your build, so a wrong hint fails the pull request, not production. And keep hints honest.

check.q: A function can return None but is hinted as returning Trip. What happens?
opts: Python raises an error at runtime
The checker trusts the hint and misses bugs
The hint is auto-corrected
check.why: Checkers trust declared types, so a dishonest hint hides real None bugs.

work: Add a type checker step to your CI so wrong hints fail the pull request.
Replace list of dict with a TypedDict or dataclass where keys matter.

reels.title: How strict, and where

beats.say: Should every function in your codebase be fully typed?

Mostly yes, and strictness should rise with the code's lifespan and reach. Shared libraries, pipeline interfaces, and anything other teams call deserve strict checking. A throwaway notebook does not. Adopt it gradually, module by module, and fail the build only on typed code.

Hints are not validation. They vanish at runtime, so data arriving from files or APIs still needs real checking with something like Pydantic, which enforces the types when data enters the system. Hints cover your code. Validation covers the outside world.

In AI work, hints double as contracts. Tool frameworks read your signature to tell the model what arguments a tool takes. A vague type means a vague tool, and the model guesses. Precise types are cheap, and they steer the model.

show.title: Hints as tool schemas
items: Vague type, vague tool, model guesses

check.q: Data arrives from an external API with unknown quality. What protects you?
opts: Type hints alone
Runtime validation like Pydantic at the boundary
A bigger mypy strictness setting
check.why: Hints vanish at runtime, so untrusted input needs real validation where it enters.

work: Pick strict checking for shared libraries and loosen it for scratch code.
Validate external data at the boundary, then trust the typed core.
Give agent tool functions precise hints so the generated schema is clear.

reels.title: The kitchen that never gets rebuilt

beats.say: Ever wonder how a restaurant adds a new dish without rebuilding its kitchen?
Each person has one job. The chef cooks, the waiter serves, the cashier takes payment. If the cashier also cooks, one bad day breaks everything.
New dish? Add a recipe card. Nobody rewrites the kitchen rules. A design round gives you about an hour to build something small, like a parking lot, using this same habit.

show.title: The habit
items: Add a card, do not rewrite rules
Swap a chef, nothing else changes
Small system, built in an hour

check.q: In the restaurant analogy, what does adding a new dish by adding a recipe card represent?
opts: Rewriting the whole system
Extending behaviour by adding a new piece without editing old ones
Hiring more cashiers
Removing the waiter
check.why: Adding a card leaves existing rules untouched, which mirrors extending software by adding a class instead of changing working code.

work: Pick one class you own and list every job it does; circle any that could be separate.
Next time you add a feature, try adding a new class or function before editing an existing branch.

reels.title: Building a parking lot in sixty minutes

beats.say: You have sixty minutes to build a parking lot. Where do you start?
Spend the first five minutes asking questions. Which operations: park, leave, pay? How many spots? What might change, like pricing?
Then split into classes. The lot finds spots. A ticket records entry time. A pricing strategy computes the fee. One class, one job.
Hourly rate, flat rate, weekend rate each become a small class with the same method. The lot calls that method and never checks which kind it is. Finish with a demo and one change request.

check.q: Why does the lot call one fee method on any pricing class instead of checking its type?
opts: It runs faster
New pricing types can be added without editing the lot
Types cannot be checked in Python
It saves memory
check.why: Because every pricing class offers the same method, the lot stays unchanged when you add a new one.

work: Practise a parking lot or rate limiter with a timer: five minutes of questions, then code.
Write down the one thing most likely to change in your design and hide it behind a small interface.

reels.title: Why working code still fails

beats.say: Why do interviewers fail candidates whose code works?
Because of the if elif chain. Every new pricing type means editing the working function, and each edit can break old cases. Open for extension, closed for modification means adding a class instead.

show.title: The smell
show.text:
if kind == 'hourly': ...
elif kind == 'flat': ...
elif kind == 'weekend': ...

beats.say: Another trap: the lot builds its own price calculator inside. Then you cannot test it with a fake. Pass in anything that matches a Protocol, which is just a list of methods it must have. That is dependency inversion.
Also ask about two cars arriving at once. Without a lock, both can grab the last spot. And do not invent ten patterns for a two-class problem.

show.title: More gotchas
items: Race: two cars, one last spot
Use a lock around spot assignment

check.q: What is the main testing benefit of passing a pricing object into the lot instead of creating it inside?
opts: Fewer lines of code
You can inject a fake with a known fee
Pricing runs in parallel
It removes the need for classes
check.why: Injected dependencies can be replaced by fakes, so you test the lot alone with predictable fees.

work: Review your last design for hidden constructors inside classes and move them to arguments.
Ask in every round what happens if two requests arrive at the same instant.

reels.title: When clean design is too much

beats.say: When is clean object design the wrong answer?

A Strategy class for every rule costs files, names and indirection. If there are two rules and they rarely change, a plain function is cheaper and easier to read. Add the pattern when the third variant appears.
Observer sounds nice for notifications, but it hides who reacts and in what order. If a subscriber fails, does the sender fail too? Decide, and say so.
Also state the limit. An in-memory design lives in one process. At many servers, you need a shared store and locks, so say what you would change. Show judgment, not pattern count.

show.title: Say the limits
items: Many servers need a shared store

check.q: When is a plain function a better choice than a Strategy class hierarchy?
opts: When there are many variants that change often
When there are very few stable rules
When you need testing
When using Protocols
check.why: With few, stable rules the extra classes add indirection without benefit; introduce the pattern once variants grow.

work: For each pattern in your design, write one sentence on the change it protects against.
End every design answer by naming what breaks at ten servers and what you would swap in.

reels.title: Parts, not family trees

beats.say: Why do engineers say build with parts, not family trees?
Think of a family tree. A child inherits from a parent, who inherited from a grandparent. Change something at the top, and every descendant feels it.

show.title: A change at the *top* ripples down

beats.say: Now think of LEGO. A car has wheels, an engine and a body. Each piece snaps in. Swap the wheels and nothing else changes.

chip.text: Swap one part, the rest stays

beats.say: Code works the same way. Composition means an object has parts. Inheritance means an object is a kind of another thing. Parts are easier to swap, so they break less.

show.title: Two ways to relate things
items: Parts swap easily and break less

check.q: A Pipeline is built from a source, steps and a sink passed in. Which idea is this?
opts: Inheritance, because Pipeline is a kind of source
Composition, because Pipeline has parts
Neither, it is just a function
check.why: The Pipeline holds other objects as parts it has, which is composition. It is not a kind of source.

work: Look at one class in your codebase and say aloud whether it is a kind of something or has something.
Find a base class with many subclasses and list what would break if you changed the base.

reels.title: How a Pipeline is composed

beats.say: How does one small class run any pipeline you can imagine?
Pipeline holds three things: a source, a list of steps, and a sink. It does no reading or writing itself. It only coordinates.
Run loops over rows. Say the source gives one thousand rows and you have three steps. Each row passes through all three steps, then the sink writes it. That is three thousand step calls.
Want to read from an API instead of a CSV? Pass a different source. The Pipeline code does not change a single line, because it only calls read.

show.title: Swap the source
show.text:
Pipeline(CsvSource(path), steps, sink)
Pipeline(ApiSource(url), steps, sink)

check.q: You switch from a CSV source to an API source. What changes in Pipeline.run?
opts: Nothing, it only calls read
You add a branch for the API
You make ApiSource inherit from CsvSource
check.why: Pipeline depends only on the read method, so any object offering it can be plugged in without touching run.

work: Rewrite one script that mixes reading, cleaning and writing so each part is a separate object or function.
Write a Pipeline test that passes a list of three dicts as the source.

reels.title: Duck typing, Protocols and gotchas

beats.say: What happens if you pass a source with no read method?

show.sub: Python will not warn you early

beats.say: Python does duck typing. It never checks the class, only whether the method exists. So the failure is an AttributeError, and it fires when run reaches that call, maybe after half your data moved.
A Protocol writes the expected method down, such as read returning rows. Your type checker catches the mistake before you run. But at runtime Python still does not enforce it, so tests matter.

show.title: Protocol
show.note: Checked by the type checker, not at runtime

beats.say: Also watch shared state. If a step keeps a counter inside itself, two pipelines using that step will mix their numbers. And a source that returns a generator can be read only once.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Protocol checks happen in the type checker only
Steps holding state get shared by reuse
Generators are consumed after one read

check.q: You add a Protocol called Source and run with an object lacking read. When does it fail?
opts: At class definition, Python enforces Protocols
In the type checker if you run one, otherwise at runtime when read is called
Never, Python skips missing methods
check.why: Protocols are for static checkers. Python itself only fails with AttributeError when the missing method is actually called.

work: Run a type checker such as mypy in CI so Protocol mistakes fail before deploy.
Make steps stateless, or build a fresh one per pipeline.
Have sources return a fresh iterator on each read call.

reels.title: When to compose, when to inherit

beats.say: When is inheritance still the right answer?
Use it for one shallow level: an abstract base that holds shared logic, like retries, with subclasses filling in one method. Python then refuses to build a subclass that forgets it.

chip.text: Shared logic, one method to fill

beats.say: Choose composition when behaviours vary independently, like source, rules and sink. Three sources times four sinks is twelve subclasses, but only seven parts when composed.
The cost is wiring and indirection. Someone must assemble the parts, and a stack trace crosses many small objects. For a one-off script, a plain function beats both.

show.title: Costs of composition
items: Tiny scripts do not need either

beats.say: The reward is testing. You pass in a fake source with ten rows and need no real system.

check.q: You have 3 sources and 4 sinks that vary independently. What is the best design?
opts: 12 subclasses, one per pair
One base class with flags for every case
Compose a pipeline from 3 source and 4 sink parts
check.why: Composition needs only 7 parts that combine freely, while subclassing multiplies into 12 and grows with each addition.

work: Limit inheritance in your code to one level from an abstract base.
Inject sources and sinks into jobs so tests can pass in fakes.
Before adding a class, ask if a plain function would do.
